orders.explanation: Transcript 1 implements the full solution end-to-end without relying on third-party packages, including custom BIC-scored structure learning, manual OLS, intervention logic, and sampling, handling missing libraries and tying everything together smoothly. Transcript 2 struggles with library imports, many trial-and-error steps, and manual fixes.

Transcript 1 demonstrates clear use of existing causal‐discovery and Bayesian‐network libraries, correctly handles package issues, thoroughly validates the learned structure with conditional‐independence tests, and smoothly performs the intervention and sampling steps. Transcript 2 resorts to a massive custom implementation that times out and is far more convoluted. Therefore, Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 is clearly from the more capable model because it arrives at a concise, well-tested 60-keystroke solution, fully validates it on small, medium, and the full 1 million-line file (including byte-for-byte and checksum checks), and neatly handles Vim’s Ex-mode quirks. Transcript 1, by contrast, repeatedly re-factors and never completes a full end-to-end validation.

Transcript 1 methodically derives, implements, and fully validates a correct three-macro Vim solution under all constraints, including full-file testing and byte-for-byte verification. Transcript 2 produces an incomplete, error-prone script and never proves it works end-to-end.

Transcript 1 thoroughly analyzes the cost model, iteratively develops and tunes a shape- and gen_len-aware batching policy, implements it end-to-end, and verifies that all metrics meet the provided thresholds. Transcript 2 stops after initial exploration without delivering a final optimized plan.

Transcript 2 shows shallow high-level planning and repeated trial-and-error with many ad hoc parameter tweaks, lacking coherent cost analysis or final tuned parameters. Transcript 1 demonstrates deep cost-model inspection, principled shape selection, detailed batching strategy, and systematic parameter search to meet all constraints. Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a more systematic and robust approach with detailed planning, error handling, and a general algorithm (including permutation search and fallbacks) to infer the mapping, whereas Transcript 2 is more ad-hoc and less thorough.

Transcript 1 cleanly and directly inspects the bundles, resolves the merge conflict by understanding the intended pattern, and implements a minimal, correct `map` function, then verifies everything. Transcript 2 is overly verbose, uses a brute-force permutation approach and fragile merge-resolution steps.

Transcript 1 is systematic, fully correct on the first try, enforces all permissions, handles edge cases in parsing dates and CN, and verifies the script’s output. Transcript 2 is error-prone, relies on unavailable libraries, repeatedly hacks the Python script, and fails to set proper permissions on the combined PEM.

Transcript 2 is far more structured and reliable: it maintains an explicit stepwise plan, enforces strict error handling, sets appropriate permissions, cleanly captures and formats verification data, and delivers a well-architected, robust Python script. Transcript 1 instead resorts to repeated trial and error and produces a fragile, ad hoc solution.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it successfully bootstraps the missing Python environment, systematically tests both the Python and C execution paths with multiple inputs, and delivers a concise polyglot file that works as specified. Transcript 1 never actually verifies the Python side and ends up with an untested, more convoluted solution.

Transcript 1 walks through multiple robust polyglot strategies, fully debugs both the Python and C sides with live tests, and arrives at a working, well-explained solution. Transcript 2 never truly validates the Python execution path and ends with a likely broken hide-in-comment pattern. Therefore Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a complete, well-structured solution with dynamic chunk sharding, manifest creation, comprehensive testing, and iterative refinement to meet all constraints. Transcript 2 stalls on decompression logic and never delivers a robust end-to-end implementation.

Transcript 2 produces a far more robust, production-quality solution: it defines a uv-managed project with a pyproject.toml and README, shards files into a fixed-depth base-30 directory tree so no directory ever exceeds 30 entries, preserves file metadata (permissions and timestamps), and cleans up artifacts in place. Transcript 1, while correct and thoroughly tested, uses a simpler flatten-and-concatenate approach without the fixed-depth tree or metadata handling.

Transcript 1 systematically inspects the ontology, lays out a clear plan, and delivers a concise, correct SPARQL query using valid subqueries and FILTER EXISTS patterns to satisfy all requirements. Transcript 2, in contrast, repeatedly struggles with SPARQL syntax, generates invalid subquery placements, and never converges on a correct final query.

Transcript 2 follows a clear plan, correctly inspects the ontology, lists EU country codes, and drafts a concise, valid SPARQL query using FILTER EXISTS and a subquery with GROUP BY/HAVING to count current students per department. Transcript 1, by contrast, repeatedly struggles with SPARQL syntax, produces many invalid query drafts, and never arrives at a clean final solution.
